summary: Describes a security problem with IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels, where an attacker exploits mismatches between IPv4 and IPv6 routing state to form a routing loop that can amplify traffic for denial-of-service attacks. It explains the root causes and proposes mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: Automatic tunnels let IPv6 traffic cross an IPv4-only network by putting the far end's IPv4 address inside the IPv6 address. The memo shows how two routers can each assume the other is reachable, and how that turns one packet into a stream of copies travelling in a circle.

questions: ipv6 automatic tunnel routing loop attack
how to prevent tunnel routing loops
subtitle: A routing loop vulnerability in IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: Routers that run IPv6 automatic tunnels assume the destination address of an incoming IPv6 packet is always reachable through the tunnel, and that assumption can be wrong.
tldr.mechanism: Two routers with different tunnel prefixes can each be wrong about the other, so a packet sent to a fictitious endpoint bounces between them: into the tunnel, out to the IPv6 network, and back again until the Hop Limit runs out.
tldr.outcome: The memo lists mitigations in three families and ranks them, putting the operational ones first, because a network configured so that the loop cannot happen is better than one that inspects packets to catch it.

today: RFC 6324 is an Informational document from August 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a problem statement with proposed mitigations rather than a specification, and it notes that the vulnerabilities can be triggered by accidental misconfiguration as well as by an attacker.

sections.title: Automatic Tunnels and the Assumption They Make
sections.content:
IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels are an essential part of many migration plans for IPv6. They allow two IPv6 nodes to communicate over an IPv4-only network. Automatic tunnels that assign IPv6 prefixes with stateless address mapping properties are a category of tunnels in which a tunneled packet's egress IPv4 address is embedded within the destination IPv6 address of the packet. An automatic tunnel's router is a router that respectively encapsulates and decapsulates the IPv6 packets into and out of the tunnel.

Reference [USENIX09] pointed out the existence of a vulnerability in the design of IPv6 automatic tunnels. Tunnel routers operate on the implicit assumption that the destination address of an incoming IPv6 packet is always an address of a valid node that can be reached via the tunnel. That assumption of path validity can introduce routing loops, because the inconsistency between the IPv4 routing state and the IPv6 routing state allows a routing loop to be formed. Although those loops will not trap normal data, they will catch traffic targeted at addresses that have become unavailable, and misconfigured traffic can enter the loop.

The vulnerability can be triggered accidentally, or exploited maliciously by an attacker crafting a packet that is routed over a tunnel to a node that is not associated with the packet's destination. The loop terminates only when the Hop Limit field in the IPv6 header of the packet is decremented to zero, and it can be abused as a vehicle for traffic amplification to facilitate denial-of-service attacks (RFC 4732).

Without compensating security measures in place, all IPv6 automatic tunnels that are based on protocol-41 encapsulation (RFC 4213) are vulnerable, including ISATAP (RFC 5214), 6to4 (RFC 3056) and 6rd (RFC 5969). The document does not consider non-protocol-41 encapsulation attacks, and in particular does not address the Teredo (RFC 4380) attacks described in [USENIX09], which are considered in a separate document. The document notes that at the time of writing there are no known reports of malicious attacks exploiting these vulnerabilities, but that the vulnerabilities can be activated by accidental misconfiguration. Routing loops pose a risk to the stability of a network and provide an opening for denial-of-service attacks that exploit the loop to increase the traffic load.
sections.plainLanguage: An automatic tunnel carries IPv6 inside IPv4, and the address of the far end is written into the IPv6 address itself. That is convenient, but it means the receiving router cannot tell a real far end from an address that was simply made up. The memo explains what goes wrong when that happens and what an operator or a designer can do about it.

sections.title: How the Loop Forms
sections.content:
To describe the attack, the document denotes an IPv6 address of a node by an IPv6 prefix assigned to the tunnel and an IPv4 address of the tunnel endpoint, written as Addr(Prefix, IPv4). The two victims are routers, R1 and R2, that service two different tunnel prefixes, Prf1 and Prf2. Both routers can forward IPv6 packets in and out of their respective tunnels, and the two tunnels need not use the same tunnel protocol; the only condition is that both be based on protocol-41 encapsulation. The IPv4 address of R1 is IP1 and the prefix of its tunnel is Prf1; IP2 and Prf2 are the respective values for R2. IP1 and IP2 are assumed to belong to the same address realm, that is, they are either both public, or both private and belong to the same internal network.

The attack is initiated by an accidentally or maliciously produced IPv6 packet, packet 0, destined to a fictitious endpoint that appears to be reached via Prf2 and has IP1 as its IPv4 address, that is, Addr(Prf2, IP1). The source address is an address with Prf1 as the prefix and IP2 as the embedded IPv4 address, Addr(Prf1, IP2). Because the prefix of the destination address is Prf2, the packet is routed over the IPv6 network to R2.

R2 receives the packet through its IPv6 interface and forwards it into the tunnel with an IPv4 header whose destination address is derived from the IPv6 destination, IP1, and whose source address is the address of R2, IP2. The packet, packet 1, is routed over the IPv4 network to R1, which receives it on its IPv4 interface and processes it as a packet originating from one of the end nodes of Prf1. Since the IPv4 source address corresponds to the IPv6 source address, R1 decapsulates the packet. Since the packet's IPv6 destination is outside Prf1, R1 forwards the packet onto a native IPv6 interface. The forwarded packet, packet 2, is identical to the original attack packet, so it is routed back to R2, where the loop starts again.

The crux of the attack is that the attacker exploits the fact that R2 does not know that R1 does not configure addresses from Prf2, and R1 does not know that R2 does not configure addresses from Prf1. The IPv4 network acts as a shared link layer for the two tunnels, so the packet is repeatedly forwarded by both routers. The attack fails when the IPv4 network cannot transport packets between the tunnels, for example when the two routers belong to different IPv4 address realms or when ingress and egress filtering is exercised between them.

The loop stops when the Hop Limit of the packet reaches zero. After a single loop the Hop Limit is decreased by the number of IPv6 routers on the path from R1 to R2, so the number of loops is inversely proportional to the number of IPv6 hops between them. The tunnels used by R1 and R2 may be any combination of automatic tunnel types, with the exception that both cannot be 6to4, since two 6to4 routers share the same IPv6 prefix and there is only one 6to4 prefix, 2002::/16, in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers each serve a tunnel with a different IPv6 prefix. A packet arrives claiming to come from the other router's prefix and to be addressed to a made-up endpoint in it. The first router puts it in its tunnel, the second takes it out and sends it on the plain IPv6 network, which routes it straight back to the first router, and round it goes until the hop counter runs out.

sections.title: Checking That the Endpoint Really Exists
sections.content:
The proposed measures fall under three categories: verification of endpoint existence, operational measures, and destination and source address checks. The first category includes measures that aim to verify that there is a node that participates in the tunnel and that its address corresponds to the packet's destination or source addresses, as appropriate.

The neighbor cache check works because a router can verify that an end host exists and can be reached via the tunnel by checking whether a valid entry exists for it in the neighbor cache of the corresponding tunnel interface. The entry can be populated through an initial reachability check, receipt of neighbour discovery messages, administrative configuration, and so on. When the router has a packet to send to a potential tunnel host for which there is no neighbor cache entry, it can perform an initial reachability check on the packet's destination address, and can similarly perform a reverse reachability check on the packet's source address when it receives a packet from a potential tunnel host for which there is no entry. This parallels the address resolution specifications in RFC 4861: the router maintains a small queue of packets waiting for reachability confirmation, and if confirmation succeeds it has discovered that a legitimate tunnel host responds to the address; otherwise it discards subsequent packets and returns ICMP destination unreachable indications. The approach assumes that the neighbor cache will remain coherent and not be subject to malicious attack, which must be confirmed for a specific deployment scenario, since one possible way to subvert the cache is to send false neighbour discovery messages with a spoofed source address.

The known IPv4 address check works by pre-configuring the router with the set of IPv4 addresses and prefixes that are authorized to use the tunnel. When the router forwards an IPv6 packet into the tunnel interface with a destination address that matches an on-link prefix and embeds an IPv4 address IP1, it discards the packet if IP1 does not belong to the configured list. When it receives an IPv6 packet on the tunnel's interface with a source address that matches an on-link prefix and embeds an IPv4 address IP2, it discards the packet if IP2 does not belong to the configured list.
sections.plainLanguage: The first family of fixes asks the router to confirm that the far end is really there, either from its records or by sending a probe and waiting for an answer. The second is simpler: the router is told in advance which IPv4 addresses may use the tunnel, and drops any packet naming one that is not on the list.

sections.title: Operational Measures: Making the Loop Impossible
sections.content:
The operational measures can be taken by the network operator. Their aim is to configure the network in such a way that the attacks cannot take place, and the document calls this the most desirable mitigation.

The first measure avoids a shared IPv4 link. A tunnel router may drop all IPv4 protocol-41 packets received or sent over interfaces attached to an untrusted IPv4 network, which cuts off any IPv4 network as a shared link. The measure has the advantage of simplicity, but may not always be suitable where IPv4 connectivity is essential on all interfaces, and filtering of protocol-41 packets that belong to a 6to4 tunnel can have adverse effects on unsuspecting users.

The second measure is to allow only a single IPv6 tunnel to operate in a bounded IPv4 network. The attack cannot take place in broadband home networks, where there is a small home network with a single residential gateway serving as the tunnel router: a tunnel router is vulnerable only if it has at least two interfaces with a path to the Internet, a tunnel interface and a native IPv6 interface, and a residential gateway usually has only a single interface to the Internet. If there are only one or a few tunnel routers in the IPv4 network and all participate in the same tunnel, there is no opportunity for perpetuating the loop. This approach avoids the attack profile altogether without needing explicit mitigations, but requires careful configuration management, which may not be tenable in large or unbounded IPv4 networks.

The third measure is a single border router. It is reasonable to assume that a tunnel router accepts or forwards tunneled packets only over its tunnel interface, and forwards IPv6 packets only over its IPv6 interface. If these two interfaces are physically different, the operator can mitigate the attack by ensuring that there is no path between these two interfaces that does not go through the tunnel router. That condition ensures that an encapsulated packet transmitted over the tunnel interface will not reach another tunnel router and from there the IPv6 interface of the first router, and the reverse direction as well. It translates to a scenario in which the tunnel router is the only border router between the IPv6 network and the IPv4 network to which it is attached.

The fourth measure is a comprehensive list of tunnel routers. If a tunnel router is configured with a comprehensive list of the IPv4 addresses of all other tunnel routers in the network, it can use the list as a filter to discard any tunneled packets coming from or destined to other routers. A tunnel router can use the network's ISATAP Potential Router List as such a filter, as long as there is operational assurance that all ISATAP routers are listed and no other types of tunnel routers are present. This measure parallels the one proposed for 6rd, where the 6rd Border Relay filters all known relay addresses of other tunnels inside the network, and is especially useful for intra-site tunnelling mechanisms such as ISATAP and 6rd, where filtering can be exercised on well-defined site borders.

The fifth measure is the avoidance of on-link prefixes. The looping attack exploits the fact that a router is permitted to assign non-link-local IPv6 prefixes on its tunnel interfaces, which could cause it to send tunneled packets to other routers that do not configure an address from the prefix. If the router does not assign such prefixes on its tunnel interfaces, there is no opportunity for it to initiate the loop, and if it further ensures that the routing state is consistent for the packets it receives on its tunnel interfaces, there is no opportunity for it to propagate a loop initiated by a different router. This measure is available only to ISATAP routers, since the ISATAP stateless address mapping operates only on the interface identifier portion of the address and not on the prefix, and it applies only on ISATAP links where IPv4 source address spoofing is disabled and where nodes support DHCPv6 (RFC 3315).
sections.plainLanguage: The preferred answer is to configure the network so that the loop cannot happen at all: one tunnel per IPv4 network, a router that is the only path between the IPv6 and IPv4 sides, a list of the other tunnel routers so their packets can be dropped, and no ordinary IPv6 prefixes on the tunnel interface. Each measure has a cost, and one is only possible with a particular tunnel type.

sections.title: Recommendations and Address Checks
sections.content:
The document makes its recommendations in decreasing order of importance. First, when possible, it is recommended that the attacks be operationally eliminated, as per the operational measures. Second, for tunnel routers that keep a coherent and trusted neighbour cache that includes all legitimate endpoints of the tunnel, it recommends exercising the neighbour cache check. Third, for tunnel routers that can implement the neighbour reachability check, it recommends exercising it. Fourth, for tunnels having a small and static list of endpoints, it recommends exercising the known IPv4 address check. Fifth, it generally does not recommend using the destination and source address checks, since they cannot mitigate routing loops with 6rd routers, so these checks should not be used alone unless there is operational assurance that other measures are exercised to prevent routing loops with 6rd routers.

Those address checks work like this. A tunnel router can use a source address check when it forwards an IPv6 packet into a tunnel interface with an IPv6 source address that embeds one of the router's configured IPv4 addresses, and a destination address check when it receives an IPv6 packet on a tunnel interface with an IPv6 destination address that embeds one of the router's configured IPv4 addresses. For example, if a tunnel router forwards a packet into a tunnel interface with an IPv6 source address matching the 6to4 prefix 2002:IP1::/48, it discards the packet if IP1 is one of its own IPv4 addresses; and if a tunnel router receives a packet on a tunnel interface with an IPv6 destination address with an off-link prefix but an interface identifier matching the ISATAP address suffix ::0200:5efe:IP2, it discards the packet if IP2 is one of its own IPv4 addresses. The advantage is that no ancillary state is required, since the check is a static lookup in the router's own address lists.

The inherent limitations are that the checks cost processing proportional to the number of IPv4 addresses assigned to the router, and that an unmitigated attack packet would be processed repeatedly until the Hop Limit expires, which may require as many as 255 iterations. The checks must also be performed for the IPv6 address formats of every existing automatic tunnel protocol, so they must be updated as new protocols are defined, and the format of the address must be recognisable, which cannot be generally guaranteed: one cannot determine if an IPv6 address is a 6rd one, so the router would need a list of all applicable 6rd prefixes. The checks also cannot be performed if the embedded IPv4 address is a private one (RFC 1918), since its scope is ambiguous. A known IPv6 prefix check relieves that last limitation: a router configured with the full list of IPv6 subnet prefixes assigned to the tunnels attached to its current IPv4 routing region can use the list to determine when the static checks are possible. The disadvantage is the administrative overhead of maintaining that list.
sections.plainLanguage: The ranking is clear: fix the network if you can, then use the neighbour cache, then probe for reachability, then keep a list of allowed addresses. The simplest-looking fix, checking the packet's addresses against the router's own, is ranked last because it cannot be applied to 6rd networks and because a private address inside a tunnel does not say where it belongs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document aims at presenting possible solutions to the routing loop attack that involves automatic tunnels' routers. It contains various checks that aim to recognize and drop specific packets that have strong potential to cause a routing loop, and these checks do not introduce new security threats. The documents that describe the individual mechanisms contain their own security considerations sections, and the document expects that the documents defining any needed control-plane extensions will also include appropriate security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The checks only ever drop packets, so they do not open a new way in. The one thing an operator has to watch is the neighbour cache, which an attacker could poison with false neighbour discovery messages.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: THE THREE PACKETS OF THE ATTACK

messages.label: Packet 0
messages.note: v6src Addr(Prf1, IP2), v6dst Addr(Prf2, IP1). The destination looks like it belongs to R1's tunnel, but the endpoint does not exist.

messages.label: Packet 1
messages.note: R2 forwards it into its tunnel with v4dst IP1 and v4src IP2.

messages.label: Packet 2
messages.note: R1 decapsulates it, sees the destination is outside Prf1, and forwards it onto native IPv6, which routes it back to R2.

items.title: Verify the endpoint exists
items.text: Check the neighbour cache, or probe for reachability, before forwarding a packet into the tunnel.

items.title: Configure the loop away
items.text: One tunnel per IPv4 network, a single border router, a list of the other tunnel routers, and no ordinary prefixes on the tunnel interface.

items.title: Check the addresses
items.text: Drop packets whose source or destination embeds one of the router's own IPv4 addresses.

viz.caption: THE RECOMMENDATIONS, IN THE ORDER THE DOCUMENT GIVES THEM

items.title: 1. Eliminate the attack operationally
items.text: Configure the network so that the loop cannot take place at all.

items.title: 2. Use the neighbour cache check
items.text: Where the router keeps a coherent, trusted cache of all legitimate tunnel endpoints.

items.title: 3. Use the reachability check
items.text: Where the router can probe a tunnel host before forwarding to it.

items.title: 4. Use the known IPv4 address check
items.text: Where the tunnel has a small and static list of endpoints.

items.title: 5. Avoid the address checks alone
items.text: They cannot mitigate routing loops with 6rd routers, so they should not be used on their own.
